title: Transposition and Material Implication (Trans, Impl)
short: Trans: p → q :: ¬q → ¬p. Impl: p → q :: ¬p ∨ q.
trouble: Learners transpose without negating both sides, or write Impl as p ∨ ¬q.

blocks.html: Two rules of replacement deal with conditionals. Transposition (Trans) turns a conditional into its contrapositive, which you know is equivalent from Converse, Inverse and Contrapositive. Material implication (Impl) turns a conditional into a disjunction. They extend Commutation, Association and Distribution (Com, Assoc, Dist).
Trans: a conditional may be replaced by its contrapositive (swap the parts and negate both), and back. Impl: $p \to q$ may be replaced by $\neg p \lor q$, and back.

Both pairs have the same truth table: $p o q$, $ eg q o eg p$ and $ eg p \lor q$ are each false only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false. Impl says a conditional amounts to "either the antecedent fails or the consequent holds", which is the promise reading of Truth Values of the Connectives in other words. These rules let you move between conditionals and disjunctions, so MP, MT, DS and HS can all reach the same information.

blocks.title: Transposition
steps:
Swap the parts and negate both: $
eg 
eg s 	o 
eg r$.
DN may then simplify $\neg \neg s$ to $s$ in another step.

blocks.title: Material implication
blocks.q: Apply Impl to $\neg p \lor q$ to get a conditional.
steps: Read Impl right to left: $\neg p \lor q$ :: $p \to q$.

blocks.title: Impl in a proof
blocks.q: Premises $p \to q$ and $\neg q \lor r$. Prove $p \to r$.
steps: Line 3: $q \to r$ by Impl 2 (since $\neg q \lor r$ :: $q \to r$).

blocks.html: Transposing without negating both sides (that gives the converse $q \to p$, which is not equivalent), or writing Impl as $p \lor \neg q$. Impl negates the antecedent: $p \to q$ :: $\neg p \lor q$. A quick check: put $p$ T, $q$ F into your result. It must come out F, as the conditional does.

blocks.title: Trans in a proof
blocks.q: Premises $p \to q$ and $\neg q \to r$. Prove $\neg p \to r$?
steps: Careful: HS needs the consequent of one conditional to be the antecedent of the other.
Trans turns $p \to q$ into $\neg q \to \neg p$, which chains with nothing here.

Instead, Trans on $
eg q 	o r$ gives $
eg r 	o 
eg 
eg q$; that does not help either.
blocks.a: This argument is actually invalid (try $p$ F, $q$ T, $r$ F). Not every pair of conditionals chains.

blocks.title: Trans that works
blocks.q: Premises $p \to q$ and $\neg p \to r$. Prove $\neg q \to r$.
blocks.a: Trans made the consequent $\neg p$ match the antecedent of premise 2.

blocks.html: The lesson of that example: before reshaping, check that the argument is valid. A short truth table takes a minute and can save a long search for a proof that does not exist.

Impl also explains why $p \lor q$ is equivalent to $ eg p o q$: replace $p$ by $ eg p$ in the rule, giving $ eg p o q$ :: $ eg eg p \lor q$, and DN finishes the job. Translating "unless" as $\lor$ in Translating Conditionals rested on exactly this equivalence.
